limitations: The proposed model is a mathematical combination of different sub-models; therefore, its validity and accuracy are strictly correlated to those of the original models.
The proposed model is validated only for the low level of metabolic rates, and further development is needed to extend it to different cases.

Due to the complexity of the interaction of visual and non-visual photoreceptors and the ambiguities in light-induced thermal responses, it is necessary to conduct further experimental studies to evaluate more accurately the performance of the proposed model.

Future research will aim to corroborate the model and its validity through experimental campaigns, where the effect of light spectral properties on the heart rate and the body's thermoregulatory parameters under several controlled climatic conditions will be tested.
Due to the high sensitivity of physiological parameters, the selection of the measuring instruments with appropriate accuracy becomes crucial.

The linear approximation used to calculate the equivalent metabolic rate makes this model applicable to cases where low physical activities are considered, such as at rest or during sedentary work. Further experiments are necessary to validate its accuracy for higher physical activity.
minimum_safe_summary: This paper introduces a novel theoretical method to predict the effects of lighting colour temperature (CCT) on human physiological responses and indoor thermal perception. It proposes an 'equivalent metabolic rate' parameter to integrate hue-heat effects into existing thermal comfort models (PMV and Gagge's two-node model). The modified models were validated against published experimental data, showing good agreement. Numerical simulations predict that deviations from CCT 5000 K alter thermal sensation and evoke thermophysiological responses, with maximum effects observed at 4000 K and minimum at 6500 K. Thermal perception is more sensitive to CCT changes in warm environments, with potential changes up to 0.8 units in thermal sensation and up to 0.8°C in skin temperature. Limitations include validation only for low metabolic rates and the need for further experimental studies to account for complex visual and non-visual photoreceptor interactions and higher physical activities.
